a84.t:
Three years ago, Thomas Kazungu Karisa was struggling to make ends meet as a petrol station attendant in the Kenyan county of Kilifi, when a sudden cash donation changed his life.
“My family often went to bed hungry, my children were sent home from school for unpaid fees and I was buried in debt,” said Karisa, a father of five.
Now he beams at his lush farm blooming with okra, the result of a one-off donation of 110,000 Kenyan shillings (roughly $930 at the time) from a New York-based NGO, GiveDirectly.
He used the cash to lease a plot of land with two neighbours in his village of Milore, install an irrigation system and start farming.
He built up credit and bought two cows, as well as a chainsaw he rents out for 2,000 Kenyan shillings at a time.
“If they had given me food, it would have been long gone by now,” Karisa told AFP.
“But with the money, I have been able to change my life.”
GiveDirectly believes charities and NGOs should stop handing out things like food and school books, and start just sending people cash.
It has given donations to almost 1.5 million Africans, and has carried out 25 studies across the continent to measure the impact.
Fears the money would be misused or wasted were unfounded, it said. One Kenyan study found that families generated $2.50 for every $1 received.
“We can show evidence of cash having reversed domestic violence, improved child mortality, improved business outcomes, made families healthier, children accessing more education,” said Caroline Teti, GiveDirectly’s vice president for risk in Africa.
‘Poverty doesn’t wait’
With the United States and other Western countries sharply cutting aid in recent months, GiveDirectly believes cash handouts offer a way to do more with less.
Traditional aid systems spend vast amounts on planning, supplies, transport, offices and expensive Western staff.
A 2022 study by the University of Washington found that back-office costs in the United States ate up 30 to 60 percent of budgets for global health projects. Much more was lost getting supplies to the final endpoint.
GiveDirectly still has overhead costs, but says 80 percent of donations goes directly into the hands of recipients.
“Cash is not a magic bullet,” Teti said. Governments are still needed for fundamentals like schools, health facilities and electricity.
But for improving livelihoods of the poor, cash can be effective and fast.
“Poverty doesn’t wait,” Teti said. “One year is enough for a girl to drop out of school… for a mother or child to die.”
Other aid agencies have embraced the concept over the past 10-15 years as hundreds of studies have shown its efficacy.
The Norwegian Refugee Council now gives 20 percent of its aid in cash, but could easily give as much as 45 percent, said Tariq Riebl, its strategy and innovation director.
Even USAID — before being gutted by the administration of President Donald Trump — finally backed the use of cash payments in a policy paper last October, after years of internal pushback.
The only real obstacle, Riebl told AFP, is “latent conservatism” in the aid sector: “There’s something more comforting about handing over a kit of non-food items or a sack of rice, than giving cash.”
‘Dilemma’
Cash is not suitable everywhere, such as war zones where markets barely exist, or when specialist items are needed like ID cards for refugees, or HIV medication.
Doctors Without Borders (MSF), a medical organisation, has twice used cash transfers when markets collapsed: in Syria in the mid-2010s and recently in Sudan’s Darfur region.
But they were exceptions.
“Cash for healthcare remains very rare,” said MSF’s advocacy head, Tarak Bach Baouab. “We want to be sure of the quality of our programmes so we prefer sourcing the drugs and equipment ourselves.”
Nonetheless, there is a dilemma.
“We’re not there to tell people what to do with their lives. It’s not very empowering and it creates a lot of dependency,” Baouab said.
“But if you give cash to a family and they don’t spend it in the right way, then we might see health outcomes diminish.”
GiveDirectly sees this as a selling point for giving cash wherever possible.
“Lives can only be changed by the people who are living that life,” Teti said.
“We are giving them dignity and we are giving them choice.”

a156.t:
La Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS) a organisé, le mercredi 2 juin 2021 à Niassan dans la province du Sourou (Tougan), une journée d’information et de sensibilisation des responsables des structures faîtières des organisations agro-sylvo-pastorales et du secteur informel de la vallée du Sourou sur l’assurance volontaire. L’objectif de cette journée était de susciter des souscriptions. La journée a été animée par le Chef de service promotion de l’assurance volontaire, Toussaint Bationo. La mission de la CNSS était placée sous l’autorité du Directeur régional de Dédougou.
Cette journée d’information et de sensibilisation des structures faîtières s’inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du plan triennal 2020-2022 de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS). A travers cette campagne, la CNSS entend, entre autres, informer et sensibiliser les responsables des structures faîtières de la vallée du Sourou sur
l’assurance volontaire et de recueillir leurs attentes et leurs préoccupations sur ce produit dans la perspective de susciter une adhésion massive à l’assurance volontaire. Selon le Directeur régional de la CNSS de la Boucle du Mouhoun, Salifou Lougué, la vallée du Sourou n’est pas un choix fortuit.
Il est constaté, selon les explications de Salifou Lougué, que cette localité regorge d’acteurs exerçant des activités libérales sans savoir assurer leurs vieux jours. C’est pour cette raison que la CNSS, a-t-il poursuivi, a initié cette journée pour leur faire comprendre l’importance de s’assurer, de faire connaître l’assurance volontaire de la CNSS et aussi de susciter leur adhésion à ce produit. Les participants ont été instruits et sensibilisés, à cet effet, à travers un exposé animé par Toussaint Bationo, Chef de service Promotion de l’assurance volontaire. L’animateur a fait savoir que selon l’article 22 de la déclaration universelle des Droits de l’Homme, toute personne a droit à la sécurité sociale en tant que membre de la société.
Le concept sécurité sociale se définit, entre autres, comme un système de protection que la société accorde à ses membres par un ensemble de mesures publiques contre la misère économique et sociale, les différents risques comme la maladie, l’invalidité, la vieillesse, le chômage, les charges familiales et le décès, a-t-il expliqué. D’où, selon lui, l’institution de la Caisse nationale de la sécurité sociale. Au Burkina Faso, a-t-il dit, le régime de sécurité sociale applicable aux travailleurs salariés et assimilés, est géré par la CNSS et régi par la loi n°015-2006/AN du 11 mai 2006. Il a en outre, décrit les prestations servies par la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale et ses sources de financement.
Assurer leurs vieux jours
Il n’y a pas que les fonctionnaires qui bénéficient d’une pension-retraite, à en croire le chef de service Promotion de l’assurance volontaire.
Le gouvernement a institué l’assurance volontaire par la loi N°015-2006/AN du 15 mai 2006 (article 4 et 5) et l’arrêté n°2008-002/MTSS/SG/DGPS du 10 mars 2008 dans l’espoir de ne pas laisser à la traîne, les acteurs des professions libérales, du secteur informel qui travaillent à leur propre compte, où qu’ils soient, a signifié Toussaint Bationo. Qui peut être assuré ? Comment devenir assuré volontaire ? Quel est le montant des cotisations à verser et les périodes de versement ? Où et comment payer les cotisations ?  Qui sont les ayants droit de l’assuré volontaire et le montant de la pension des survivants de l’assuré volontaire ? Ce sont autant de questions qui ont animé les débats de Niassan.
En conclusion, M. Bationo a indiqué que la sécurité sociale est un droit pour tout être humain, en général et pour tout Burkinabè, en particulier. Elle est également la forme de solidarité la plus élaborée avec la garantie de l’Etat. Sans être affiliée à la CNSS, l’assurance volontaire permet aux commerçants, vendeuses de légumes et fruits, détenteurs de petits restaurants ou de débits de boisson et même des vendeurs de téléphones mobiles, de cotiser de façon mensuelle ou trimestrielle afin d’assurer leurs vieux jours. Aussi, il a lancé un vibrant appel à tous ceux qui disposent d’un revenu à s’assurer afin d’éviter les lendemains qui déchantent.
Au terme de cet exposé, Toussaint Bationo et son équipe se sont soumis aux questions des participants. Ce débat a permis de recueillir les préoccupations et d’éclairer davantage la lanterne des participants. A la fin de la journée, le chef de service Promotion de l’assurance volontaire n’a pas caché sa satisfaction au regard de la mobilisation et l’engouement des
participants aux échanges et la pertinence de leurs
questions. Le président de l’Union des coopératives agricoles de la vallée du Sourou (UCAVASO), Issiaka Soro a, au nom des participants, félicité la CNSS pour cette mission. Selon lui, le chef de service Promotion de l’assurance volontaire n’a pas prêché dans le désert.
Il a convaincu plus d’un à la souscription à l’assurance volontaire. Celui-ci a par ailleurs assuré la mission que leur exhortation sera relayée à travers la vallée du Sourou.
Notons que les travaux ont connu la participation du chef d’agence de la CNSS de Tougan, Bagabila Barthelemy Kiendrebéogo, le chef du service de
recouvrement et du contentieux de la CNSS de la Boucle du Mouhoun, Mamadou Zonou et un représentant du directeur général de l’Autorité de la mise en valeur de la vallée du Sorou, Blaise Konaté. C’est sur une note de satisfaction générale que l’équipe de la CNSS a pris congé de leurs hôtes.
Paul DRABO
(AIB/Sourou)
a156.en:
Voluntary insurance: The CNSS preaches in the Sourou valley

The National Social Security Fund (CNSS) organised, on Wednesday 2 June 2021 at Niassan in the province of Sourou (Tougan), a day of information and awareness-raising for the heads of umbrella structures of agro-sylvo-pastoral organisations and of the informal sector of the Sourou valley on voluntary insurance. The objective of this day was to encourage subscriptions. The day was led by the Head of the Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service, Toussaint Bationo. The CNSS mission was placed under the authority of the Regional Director of Dedougou.

This day of information and awareness-raising for the umbrella structures forms part of the implementation of the 2020-2022 three-year plan of the National Social Security Fund (CNSS). Through this campaign, the CNSS intends, among other things, to inform and raise the awareness of the heads of the umbrella structures of the Sourou valley about voluntary insurance and to gather their expectations and concerns about this product with a view to encouraging mass adherence to voluntary insurance. According to the CNSS Regional Director for the Boucle du Mouhoun, Salifou Lougue, the Sourou valley is not a random choice.

It has been observed, according to Salifou Lougue's explanations, that this locality abounds with people carrying out self-employed activities without knowing how to provide for their old age. It is for this reason that the CNSS, he continued, initiated this day to make them understand the importance of insuring themselves, to make the CNSS's voluntary insurance known and also to encourage their adherence to this product. The participants were instructed and made aware, to this end, through a presentation given by Toussaint Bationo, Head of the Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service. The presenter pointed out that, according to Article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, everyone has the right to social security as a member of society.

The concept of social security is defined, among other things, as a system of protection that society grants to its members through a set of public measures against economic and social destitution and the various risks such as illness, disability, old age, unemployment, family burdens and death, he explained. Hence, according to him, the institution of the National Social Security Fund. In Burkina Faso, he said, the social security scheme applicable to salaried and similar workers is managed by the CNSS and governed by law n°015-2006/AN of 11 May 2006. He also described the benefits provided by the National Social Security Fund and its sources of financing.

Providing for their old age

It is not only civil servants who benefit from a retirement pension, according to the head of the Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service.

The government instituted voluntary insurance by law N°015-2006/AN of 15 May 2006 (articles 4 and 5) and by order n°2008-002/MTSS/SG/DGPS of 10 March 2008 in the hope of not leaving behind the actors of the liberal professions and of the informal sector who work on their own account, wherever they may be, indicated Toussaint Bationo. Who can be insured? How does one become a voluntary insured person? What is the amount of the contributions to be paid and the payment periods? Where and how to pay the contributions? Who are the beneficiaries of the voluntary insured person and the amount of the survivors' pension of the voluntary insured person? These are all questions that animated the debates at Niassan.

In conclusion, Mr Bationo indicated that social security is a right for every human being in general and for every Burkinabe in particular. It is also the most elaborate form of solidarity, with the guarantee of the State. Without being affiliated to the CNSS, voluntary insurance allows traders, vegetable and fruit sellers, owners of small restaurants or drinking establishments and even mobile phone sellers to contribute on a monthly or quarterly basis in order to provide for their old age. He also launched a strong appeal to all those who have an income to insure themselves in order to avoid disappointing tomorrows.

At the end of this presentation, Toussaint Bationo and his team submitted to the participants' questions. This debate made it possible to gather their concerns and to shed further light for the participants. At the end of the day, the head of the Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service did not hide his satisfaction at the turnout and the enthusiasm of the participants in the exchanges and the relevance of their questions. The president of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of the Sourou Valley (UCAVASO), Issiaka Soro, on behalf of the participants, congratulated the CNSS for this mission. According to him, the head of the Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service had not preached in the desert.

He convinced more than one person to subscribe to voluntary insurance. He also assured the mission that their exhortation would be relayed throughout the Sourou valley.

Note that the proceedings were attended by the head of the CNSS agency of Tougan, Bagabila Barthelemy Kiendrebeogo, the head of the recovery and litigation service of the CNSS of the Boucle du Mouhoun, Mamadou Zonou, and a representative of the director general of the Authority for the Development of the Sourou Valley, Blaise Konate. It was on a note of general satisfaction that the CNSS team took leave of their hosts.

Paul DRABO
(AIB/Sourou)

a177.t:
Two meetings took place on Wednesday in Maputo: one between Finance Minister Carla Loveira and the Spanish ambassador to Mozambique, Teresa Orjales, and another between the minister and US ambassador Peter Vrooman.
At the meeting, Peter Vrooman spoke about the US government’s support for the country, including the Global Fund, the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the World Food Programme (WFP).
According to the Ministry of Finance, Vrooman recalled that part of this support remains suspended by decision of Donald Trump. However, he assured that he was working to ensure continued support in areas that are crucial to the country.
In light of the statement, the Finance Minister commented that the current situation of suspension of financing creates imbalances in the proposal for the 2025 Economic and Social Plan and State Budget (PESOE).
On that occasion, the American diplomat asked about the Government’s new institutional structure. “Answering the question, the finance minister assured that it is focused on three main areas, the restructuring of the government machine; fiscal consolidation and good governance”.
During the other meeting, Teresa Orjales demonstrated her country’s openness to continue supporting Mozambique in its development policies and spoke about the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development that will take place in Seville, Spain, from June 30 to July 3, 2025. “This conference will be an opportunity to accelerate the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. It will also support the reform of the international financial architecture, it will also define the global financing agenda and advance the sustainable development goals”, said the Spanish diplomat.
In turn, Carla Loveira welcomed the Spanish Government’s willingness to continue supporting Mozambique and the invitation made for the country to participate in the Conference, as the country is a signatory to the 2030 Agenda and has participated in the reform of the international financial architecture.

a278.t:
Abidjan, Ivory Coast | THE INDEPENDENT | The latest African Economic Outlook (AEO) report indicates that foreign direct investment (FDI) flows following the recent issuance of oil exploration licenses and the investment in infrastructure development is expected to spur Uganda’s economy for most of 2018.
The African Development Bank 2018 edition of the yearly flagship report released on Wednesday indicates Uganda’s economic performance generally remained strong despite the recent slowdown in real GDP growth, which is projected to reach 5.9% in 2018, up from 4.8% in 2017 and 2.3% in 2016.
As a leading African institution, the African Development Bank is the first to provide headline numbers on Africa’s macroeconomic performance and outlook.
UGANDA SUMMARY
Economic performance and outlook
Economic performance generally remained strong despite the recent slowdown in real GDP growth, which is projected to reach 5.9% in 2018, up from 4.8% in 2017 and 2.3% in 2016. The increase in economic growth in 2018 is expected to be driven mainly by public infrastructure investment; recovery in manufacturing and construction; and improvements in the services sector, particularly financial and banking, trade, transport, and information and communication technology services.
Macroeconomic evolution
Uganda pursued a cautious expansionary fiscal policy stance to support key infrastructure projects in transport and energy, while keeping recurrent expenditure under control.
The overall budget deficit was slightly high in 2016, improved in 2017, and is projected to increase in 2018 and 2019. The balance of payments deteriorated, mainly as the result of external economic headwinds, including low commodity prices due to slow growth in Europe and China and tightening global financial and monetary conditions.
LAUNCH VIDEO
The macroeconomic policy stance remains focused on containing inflationary pressures, enhancing exchange rate stability, and stepping up domestic resource mobilization growth by 0.5 percentage point of GDP. Uganda continues to have a low risk of debt distress. However, the debt-toGDP ratio is increasing and is projected to reach 38.6% of GDP in 2016 and 45% by 2020 from 34.1% in 2014.
At these growth rates, the debt burden is growing faster than government resources; the revenue-to-GDP ratio stands at only 13.4%. However, the most recent International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group debt sustainability analysis in 2016 gives Uganda’s risk of debt distress a low rating.
Tailwinds
The main tailwinds for the 2018 economic outlook include increased agricultural production due to better weather conditions; higher foreign direct investment (FDI) flows following the recent issuance of oil exploration licenses; and the expected decision by the government to invest in oil infrastructure development in early 2018, given the projected increase in oil prices to an average of $55 a barrel in 2017–18 from $43 a barrel in 2016.
Headwinds
Major external risks to economic performance include low commodity prices and demand for the country’s exports in major markets, appreciation of the U.S. dollar due to expected monetary tightening by the United States, tightening of global financing conditions that could discourage FDI and development assistance, adverse spillover shocks from fragile regional neighbors, and adverse environmental shocks. Major internal risks include reduced domestic revenue mobilization and higher public spending on contingencies, poor institutional capacity and governance, and weak public financial and investment management systems.
African Economic Outlook 2018 by The Independent Magazine on Scribd

a340.t:
Le Président de la République, Patrice Talon, entouré des membres du gouvernement, a présidé vendredi 13 juin 2025 à la salle du peuple du Palais de la Marina, un séminaire consacré à l’évaluation de la gouvernance locale et à l’examen des perspectives de la réforme de la décentralisation. Cette rencontre de haut niveau a rassemblé les Préfets des douze (12) départements, les Maires des soixante-dix-sept (77) communes et leurs adjoints, les Secrétaires Exécutifs des mairies ainsi que les représentants de l’Association nationale des communes du Bénin (Ancb).
Le séminaire gouvernemental, voulu par le Chef de l’État, s’inscrit dans la dynamique de consolidation des réformes engagées depuis 2016 pour optimiser et moderniser l’action publique, tant au niveau central que local. « La gouvernance décentralisée doit être le fer de lance de l’action publique, permettant la satisfaction des besoins de base et amorçant notre développement global », a déclaré le Président de la République à l’ouverture des travaux. L’objectif de la rencontre est clair : dresser un bilan à mi-parcours de la réforme structurelle de la décentralisation, en vigueur depuis trois ans, et recueillir les retours d’expérience des élus et cadres locaux, dans un esprit de critique constructive.
Reconnaissant les faiblesses et les insuffisances antérieures, le Président Patrice Talon a rappelé que la réforme visait à rompre avec les pratiques d’antan, marquées par la confusion des rôles, la mauvaise gouvernance et l’impunité. « Fallait-il continuer ainsi, ou bien prendre les décisions courageuses pour changer la donne ? Nous avons fait le choix de la réforme, et nous devons maintenant nous assurer qu’elle produise les résultats escomptés », a-t-il souligné. Le Chef de l’État a insisté sur la nécessité pour les élus et les techniciens de mieux intégrer l’esprit de la réforme, qui repose sur une séparation claire des fonctions : les élus tracent les grandes orientations, les Secrétaires Exécutifs mettent en œuvre et assurent la gestion dans le respect des règles de bonne gouvernance.
Au nom des communes, le Président de l’ANCB, Luc Sètondji Atrokpo, a exprimé sa reconnaissance à l’endroit du Chef de l’État pour l’attention constante portée aux collectivités territoriales. « Aucune commune n’est laissée pour compte. Vos actions sont visibles du Nord au Sud, de l’Est à l’Ouest en passant par le Centre », a-t-il affirmé avec conviction, saluant également la réforme du système partisan qui, selon lui, « stabilise les conseils communaux et facilite la mise en œuvre des Plans de Développement Communaux ». Néanmoins, les élus ont soumis quelques préoccupations majeures : la reprise de la délivrance des attestations de détention coutumière (ADC), en attendant la généralisation du titre foncier, afin de sécuriser les usages fonciers et soutenir les finances communales ; la clarification du statut des maires fonctionnaires de l’État, confrontés à des situations administratives complexes ; l’intégration des véhicules de fonction au patrimoine des communes, pour permettre leur réaffectation conformément aux textes. Ce séminaire, riche en échanges, marque une étape importante dans le dialogue entre l’État central et les collectivités locales, avec une volonté partagée : faire de la décentralisation un moteur réel du développement à la base.
a340.en:
President of the Republic Patrice Talon, surrounded by members of the government, chaired a seminar on Friday 13 June 2025 in the People's Hall of the Marina Palace devoted to the evaluation of local governance and to the examination of prospects for the decentralisation reform. This high-level meeting brought together the Prefects of the twelve (12) departments, the Mayors of the seventy-seven (77) communes and their deputies, the Executive Secretaries of the town halls as well as representatives of the National Association of Communes of Benin (ANCB).

The government seminar, desired by the Head of State, is part of the drive to consolidate the reforms undertaken since 2016 to optimise and modernise public action, both at central and local level. "Decentralised governance must be the spearhead of public action, making it possible to satisfy basic needs and to launch our overall development," the President of the Republic declared at the opening of the proceedings. The objective of the meeting is clear: to draw up a mid-term assessment of the structural reform of decentralisation, in force for three years, and to gather feedback from elected officials and local managers, in a spirit of constructive criticism.

Acknowledging the earlier weaknesses and shortcomings, President Patrice Talon recalled that the reform aimed to break with the practices of the past, marked by confusion of roles, bad governance and impunity. "Should we have continued like that, or rather take courageous decisions to change things? We chose reform, and we must now make sure that it produces the expected results," he stressed. The Head of State insisted on the need for elected officials and technical staff to better internalise the spirit of the reform, which rests on a clear separation of functions: elected officials set the broad orientations, and the Executive Secretaries implement and manage in compliance with the rules of good governance.

On behalf of the communes, the President of the ANCB, Luc Setondji Atrokpo, expressed his gratitude to the Head of State for the constant attention paid to local authorities. "No commune is left behind. Your actions are visible from North to South, from East to West and through the Centre," he affirmed with conviction, also welcoming the reform of the party system which, according to him, "stabilises communal councils and facilitates the implementation of the Communal Development Plans." Nevertheless, the elected officials submitted a few major concerns: the resumption of the issuance of customary landholding certificates (ADC), pending the generalisation of land titles, in order to secure land use and support communal finances; the clarification of the status of mayors who are State civil servants, faced with complex administrative situations; the integration of official vehicles into the communes' assets, to allow their reassignment in accordance with the texts. This seminar, rich in exchanges, marks an important stage in the dialogue between the central State and local authorities, with a shared will: to make decentralisation a real engine of development at the grassroots.

a373.t:
Muktasari:
- Tangu ameingia madarakani, Januari 20, mwaka huu, Trump alitia saini amri kadhaa za kiutendaji ikiwemo ya kusitisha kwa muda misaada ya kimataifa inayotolewa na shirika la USAID, jambo ambalo limesababisha mamia ya watu kupewa likizo ya bila malipo.
Dar es Salaam. Wakati Serikali ya Marekani chini ya Rais Donald Trump ikikata misaada yake kwa mataifa mengine, Balozi wa Uingereza nchini Tanzania, Marianne Young, amesema nchi yake itaendelea kutoa misaada ya kimaendeleo na kibinadamu kama sehemu muhimu ya ushirikiano wa kimataifa.
Balozi Young amebainisha hayo wakati wa mahojiano maalumu na Mwananchi Jumatatu, Februari 17, 2025, akizungumzia athari za mabadiliko ya sera za kimataifa katika misaada ya kigeni. Ameangazia athari kwa Tanzania na jumuiya ya wafadhili wa kimataifa.
Tangu ameingia madarakani, Januari 20, mwaka huu, Trump alitia saini amri kadhaa za kiutendaji ikiwemo ya kusitisha kwa muda misaada ya kimataifa inayotolewa na shirika la USAID, jambo ambalo limesababisha mamia ya watu kupewa likizo ya bila malipo.
Akizungumzia uamuzi huo wa Marekani, amesema wanatambua Marekani imesitisha utoaji misaada hadi watakapofanya tathmini, hata hivyo amesema Serikali ya Uingereza itaendeleza dhamira yake thabiti ya kutoa misaada ya kimaendeleo na kibinadamu kama sehemu muhimu ya ushirikiano wa kimataifa.
“Tunaamini kwamba hatua shirikishi kati ya washirika wa kimataifa ni muhimu kwa ajili ya kuendeleza viashiria muhimu vya maendeleo, ikiwa ni pamoja na Malengo ya Maendeleo Endelevu (SDGs),” amesema Balozi Young.
Akizungumzia namna Uingereza inavyosaidia kuziba pengo lililoachwa na Marekani, Balozi Young amesema jumuiya ya wafadhili nchini Tanzania inafuatilia kwa karibu mabadiliko hayo ili kuelewa athari zinazoweza kutokea.
Hata hivyo, amesema kwa upande wa Uingereza, wameongeza kwa kiasi kikubwa bajeti ya Taasisi ya Maendeleo ya Nchi za Nje (ODI) katika mwaka uliopita, kutoka pauni 17 milioni (Sh55 bilioni) hadi zaidi ya pauni 50 milioni (Sh163 bilioni) kwa mwaka 2024–2025.
“Mbali na ufadhili huo, pia tunatumia fedha zinazotolewa na serikali kupitia uwekezaji wa kimataifa wa Uingereza, ambayo imekuwa mdau mkuu nchini Tanzania kwa zaidi ya miaka 50. Kwa sasa, mfumo wetu una pauni 50 milioni (Sh655 bilioni), na tunalenga kuongeza hii maradufu hadi pauni milioni 200 katika miaka michache ijayo.
“Pia, tunazingatia kutumia fedha binafsi. Hili ni eneo muhimu ambapo serikali ya Uingereza inashirikiana kikamilifu na taasisi za kimataifa ili kuongeza msaada wa kifedha na kushughulikia upungufu wa ufadhili uliopo,” amesema.
Balozi Young amezungumzia namna wanavyoshirikiana na Tanzania kusukuma maslahi ya watu wao kama vile sera za kodi, kanuni za uwekezaji na changamoto nyingine, amesema Uingereza inashika nafasi ya pili kwa ukubwa wa uwekezaji kutoka nje ya nchi (FDI) hapa Tanzania.
Amesema Uingereza ina maslahi makubwa katika sekta mbalimbali, ikiwa ni pamoja na nishati, miundombinu na chakula na vinywaji. Amesema wafanyabiashara wa Uingereza hushirikiana mara kwa mara na serikali katika changamoto wanazokutana nazo wanaoingia katika soko la Tanzania.
“Hoja kuu ni pamoja na uwazi na kutabirika, hasa kuhusu madai ya kodi na uchunguzi. Tunafurahi kwamba serikali ilikubali matatizo haya na kuwezesha mijadala iliyosababisha kuanzishwa kwa Tume ya Kodi, ambayo sasa imeanza uchunguzi wake. Tunatazamia kutolewa kwa ripoti ya Tume,” amesema balozi huyo.
Alipoulizwa kama wanaridhishwa na muda unaotumiwa na Serikali kushughulikia changamoto hizo, Young amesema, kwa kutumia mfano wa kodi, serikali ilikubali haraka wasiwasi wao na kuomba mifano mahususi, ambayo walitoa mara moja pamoja na vithibitisho na takwimu zinazoshabihiana.
“Katika kujibu, serikali iliwaita haraka makamishna kuchunguza masuala hayo. Sasa tuna matumaini kwamba mapendekezo yatawasilishwa hivi karibuni na kwamba hatua madhubuti itafuata mara moja,” amesema Balozi Young.
a373.en:
Summary:
- Since he came to power on January 20 this year, Trump has signed several executive orders, including one temporarily suspending the international aid provided by the USAID agency, something that has caused hundreds of people to be placed on unpaid leave.

Dar es Salaam. While the United States government under President Donald Trump cuts its aid to other nations, the British High Commissioner to Tanzania, Marianne Young, has said her country will continue to provide development and humanitarian assistance as an important part of international cooperation.

High Commissioner Young made this clear during a special interview with Mwananchi on Monday, February 17, 2025, speaking about the effects of changes in international policies on foreign aid. She highlighted the effects on Tanzania and on the international donor community.

Since he came to power on January 20 this year, Trump has signed several executive orders, including one temporarily suspending the international aid provided by the USAID agency, something that has caused hundreds of people to be placed on unpaid leave.

Speaking about that decision by the United States, she said they recognise that the United States has suspended the provision of aid until it carries out an assessment; however, she said the British government will continue its firm commitment to providing development and humanitarian assistance as an important part of international cooperation.

“We believe that collaborative action among international partners is essential for advancing important development indicators, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),” said High Commissioner Young.

Speaking about how Britain is helping to fill the gap left by the United States, High Commissioner Young said the donor community in Tanzania is closely following those changes in order to understand the possible effects.

However, she said that on Britain's side, they substantially increased the budget of the Overseas Development Institute (ODI) in the past year, from 17 million pounds (55 billion shillings) to more than 50 million pounds (163 billion shillings) for 2024-2025.

“Apart from that funding, we also use funds provided by the government through British International Investment, which has been a major stakeholder in Tanzania for more than 50 years. At present, our portfolio has 50 million pounds (655 billion shillings), and we aim to double this to 200 million pounds in the next few years.

“Also, we are considering using private funds. This is an important area in which the British government is fully cooperating with international institutions in order to increase financial support and address the existing funding shortfall,” she said.

High Commissioner Young spoke about how they are working with Tanzania to advance the interests of their people in areas such as tax policies, investment regulations and other challenges, saying Britain ranks second in the size of foreign direct investment (FDI) here in Tanzania.

She said Britain has major interests in various sectors, including energy, infrastructure, and food and drink. She said British businesspeople regularly engage with the government over the challenges they encounter when entering the Tanzanian market.

“The main issues include transparency and predictability, especially regarding tax claims and investigations. We are pleased that the government accepted these problems and enabled discussions that led to the establishment of the Tax Commission, which has now begun its investigation. We look forward to the release of the Commission's report,” said the ambassador.

Asked whether they are satisfied with the time the government is taking to address those challenges, Young said, using the example of tax, that the government quickly accepted their concerns and asked for specific examples, which they provided immediately along with evidence and corroborating data.

“In response, the government quickly summoned the commissioners to investigate those matters. Now we are hopeful that recommendations will be submitted soon and that decisive action will follow immediately,” said High Commissioner Young.

a438.t:
Wednesday December 11, 2024
The Somali government has ramped up its efforts to repatriate nationals from foreign African countries, successfully facilitating the return of 230 citizens who were stranded or detained over the past five days.
This repatriation process, supported by the United Nations migration agency, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), took place in Libya, Madagascar, and Sudan.
Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Ahmed Moallim Fiqi called the successful repatriations a significant milestone in addressing the challenges of irregular migration and ensuring the safety of Somali nationals abroad.
"This operation highlights Somalia's unwavering commitment to its citizens and to addressing migration challenges through cooperation with our international partners," the minister said in a statement released on Thursday when the citizens returned from Libya.
The repatriation efforts, funded by the European Union and implemented by the IOM, saw most of the returnees from Libya on the Dec. 5 charter flight as young men and women under the age of 30 who had been stranded in the country for several months.
The survivors of the Madagascar boat tragedy, aged between 17 and 50, expressed immense relief at returning to safety. The foreign ministry said the survivors of the early November boat tragedy, which claimed 28 lives in the Indian Ocean off Madagascar, shared harrowing accounts of their ordeal.
On Monday, the minister also announced the successful repatriation of 22 Somali citizens who had been detained in Sudan's Dongola and Gadaref detention facilities for three months.
All the 22 individuals arrived safely in Mogadishu, marking another milestone in the ministry's efforts to protect the rights and dignity of Somali citizens abroad and combat human trafficking, Figi said.
Every year, hundreds of Somali migrants embark on perilous journeys along the Northern Mediterranean route, passing through multiple countries with hopes of reaching Europe, the IOM said.
According to the IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix report published in July, more than 1,500 Somali migrants were stranded in Libya, where many face dangerous and precarious conditions.
Insecurity, lack of food, shelter, and healthcare in Libya expose these migrants to significant risks, the IOM said, noting that thousands urgently require protection and humanitarian assistance.

a691.t:
MUBANGA LUCHEMBE
THE UPND government’s selective anti-corruption fight against the previous regime’s actors was bound to fail. The question was when would it fail and who would be embarrassed? And what’s happening to UPND’s hitherto anti-corruption campaign promise?
U.S. Ambassador Michael C. Gonzales’s recent revelation that US$20 million in American aid – intended for maize for drought relief in the nation – remained unaccounted for provides the answers.
What did surprise many socio-politico-economic observers was that despite the dire need and the skyrocketing cost of mealie-meal, this money did not translate into food security for Zambians.
If the United States provided such a significant sum, why didn’t the UPND government ensure the delivery of affordable mealie-meal to the nation? Was it so unkind to the pain of ordinary people? Or was it keeping the money for its 2026 re-election campaign?
Then came the even more startling detail; the maize procured with these funds was bought at more than 48 percent above the market price. How could such blatant financial corruption occur under the leadership of a president who was once touted as the country’s anti-corruption champion?
The irony is bitter. Are discerning Zambians now to believe that corruption is contagious – or simply resilient?
But their concern doesn’t stop at US$20 million. The truly alarming figure is the US$3 billion that Mr Gonzales claimed Zambia loses to corruption annually. That number is the heart of President Hakainde Hichilema’s leadership.
He campaigned on an anti-corruption platform, promising to clean up after the alleged excesses of former President Edgar Lungu. Citizens were told corruption would be a thing of the past once he was voted into office.
And yet, law-abiding citizens are here again – witnessing impunity and graft flourish in broad daylight under a leader who self-hyped and billed himself as the most transparent in the country’s history.
Yet, many discerning Zambians have long viewed President Hichilema’s anti-corruption rhetoric with scepticism. His decision to place the Anti-Corruption Commission and the Drug Enforcement Commission under the direct authority of his office raised red flags.
So too has his persistent refusal to publicly disclose his business partners. If they are to trust him, transparency cannot be optional – it must be the foundation of his leadership. They deserve to know who sits at his dinner table at Community House.
Lest they have forgotten, the UPND government cannot credibly investigate itself. They only know about “maizegate” because of a change in leadership in the United States. What else might still be hidden?
For now, President Hichilema owes the voting public an explanation. And yet again, the United States government lately announced a cut of US$50 million equivalent to K1.4 billion in annual aid to Zambia intended for medications and medical supplies, citing rampant theft of donor-funded drugs and the UPND governmentís failure to take decisive corrective action.
Addressing the media at the U.S Embassy in Lusaka recently, Mr Gonzales expressed disappointment over the UPND government’s inability to prevent the diversion of essential medicines meant to be distributed free of charge to the Zambian public.
Mr. Gonzales disclosed that since late 2021, U.S. investigations uncovered widespread theft of anti-retroviral, anti-malarial medications, and tuberculosis drugs supplied through American-funded programmes.
He explained that according to the findings, 95 percent of pharmacies across the country were found selling these medicines, with 45 percent specifically distributing U.S donated supplies adding that despite more than 13-months of repeated alerts and offers of technical support from the U.S, the situation remained unresolved.
He also clarified that the US$50 million was strictly part of the US$128 million funding each year for HIV, malaria, and TB interventions and not part of broader policy shifts in the United States.
The ambassador stated that while medicines would continue to be delivered until January 2026 to avoid immediate stock-outs, no more shipments would follow unless the UPND government acted decisively and indicated its willingness to support any meaningful action during the transition period.
Reacting to this, the Ministry of Health said it was taking action against the theft of donated medicines after the United States announced a major aid cut over the government’s failure to tackle the racket.
The United States announced earlier this month, that it would cut US$50 million in annual health funding to Zambia over the “systematic” theft of medicine and other supplies meant to be handed out for free to the most vulnerable but which had been found to be on sale in pharmacies.
The US embassy said the fraud was discovered in late 2021 but the UPND government had only arrested a few mid-level officials for involvement instead of tracking down the masterminds.
The ministry said an independent forensic audit had also led to the removal from office of senior officials at the medical supplies agency, including its director general, and other actions were expected. For the moment, though, President Hichilema will be up for re-election next year, so has he fulfilled his 2021 pre-electoral campaign promise to stamp out corruption?
As fate would have it, President Hichilema has a bit of a fight on his hands. The UPND flag-bearer faces an election in August next year in which his closest rival could be retired-yet-returned to active politics ex-President Lungu of the Tonse Alliance.
The two men appear matched for a presidential election rematch. President Hichilema remains popular in his party’s strongholds of Northern, North-Western, Southern and Western provinces while ex-President Lungu can count on strongholds in Central, Copperbelt, Eastern, Luapula, Lusaka and Muchinga provinces. Because of this, the presidential candidates have to appeal beyond their ethnocentric support bases, and so the next year’s presidential contest looks likely to become one of policy as much as personality.
So, there the sceptical Zambian electorates have it – President Hichilema claims he has been able to rebrand Zambia to attract investments to avoid a return to the debilitating public debt that has been restructured by his administration since assuming office in 2021.
His opponents, however, charge that he has been divisive as a national leader, and that he has allowed graft to grow thereby exacerbating the dent in the UPND’s selective anti-corruption fight.

a853.t:
Beyond the rhetoric of liberal rules-based international order, the United States of America, by its recent actions, have become the disrupter in chief of the International order, upturning not only the enduring multilateral institutions but hitting hard at its established bilateral relations.
Nigeria, which the U.S claimed to have good bilateral relations and shared values of liberal democracy, recently jolted when its long-standing entry visa modality was abruptly cut back and reduced to three months and single entry. Following on that, Washington has further tightened its noose on curbs against Nigerians with a threat to press criminal charges, warning that “we will pursue criminal charges against those that engage in visa fraud and those who bring in and harbour illegal aliens”, after it noted that “A nation without borders is not a nation”.
The U.S revisionist immigration crackdown, with its current leadership identifying it rightly or wrong as the main crux of what ails their country, is, however, riddled with discriminatory applications which disproportionately target Africans and, in the specific instance, Nigerians. It is no gainsaying that the U.S is historically the greatest beneficiary of immigration in the world, and its strength and wealth have largely flowed from its status as a melting pot, and as a global consequential super power or what former French Foreign Minister called “hyper-power”. Yet, like the proverbial biting of hands that feeds it, the U.S immigration turmoil and visa restrictions have created chaos beyond its shores. Dumping its alleged immigrants, snatched from the streets anywhere in the U.S and just anywhere in the world, has become the new face of Washington’s contemporary confusion.
Nigeria was allegedly tapped to host the U.S.’s uncanny export of its designated illegal migrants, and the refusal of Nigeria’s authority to aid Washington in its domestic policy of immigration chaos may have triggered Washington’s vendetta of Visa restrictions against Nigeria. However, beyond visa restrictions, Washington is increasingly defining Africa and Nigeria as a battleground where it hopes to push back at what it considers the so-called malignant Chinese and Russian expansive influence. Therefore, Nigeria would only seemingly matter to the U.S to the degree to which it affords a convenient platform to roll back perceived or real China and to a lesser degree, Russia’s influence in Africa.
Recently, Washington held a summit with six selected African leaders that most observers consider a clear factor of divide and rule tactics, reminiscent of the old approach of colonial domination. Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and South Africa, the continent’s most consequential powers, were snubbed, revealing Washington’s strategic roadmap to engaging Africa through favours and snubs.
The visa restriction aimed at Nigeria for her efforts to pursue independent foreign policy is only the beginning of the prospective Washington punitive measures aimed at whipping her into line. Nigeria’s current formal status of a BRICS partner is a field that Washington holds a grudge. President Trump has not hidden his hostility to the BRICS mechanism which he considers as opposed to the Washington liberal exclusionary order.
It is no gainsaying that the BRICS mechanism is not an anti-Washington/West platform but a major contribution to emerging and evolving international governance mechanism that reflects broader inclusion and participation. Not long ago, it was revealed that the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) was complicit in the extremist insurgent war in Nigeria. Despite strident denials by the U.S side of involvement, most Nigerians who have suspected that the resilience of the insurgents would not have been possible without external support were not taken in by the plausible deniability.
The visa restrictions and threats to harshly deal with prospective violators are not an isolated act of hostility by Washington, but a deliberate act in a series to highlight the U.S.’s current prejudice and the selective threat to partners that dares to pursue an independent policy. Interestingly, while Washington’s hammer at immigration is largely viewed as precipitative and even chaotic, the harsh restrictions imposed on Nigeria and Africans are certainly not the same as the welcoming gestures to Europeans. Such discriminations expose the limits of the liberal assumptions of equity, fairness and justice, just as the massacre in Gaza of Palestinians exposes the selective humanity of the West.
From a pivotal consequential power, whose supposed voice of moderation and reason should be globally acknowledged and respected, Washington has transformed into a Traumatised Revisionist and Unhinged Muddling Power (TRUMP) with a penchant to sow chaos, disorder and dent the fabric of the international landscape.
Nigeria and other Africans should continue on the path of independent foreign policy and constructive engagement with the world, including the United States of America.
Keneth Okechukwu is a public affairs analyst and contributed from Abuja.

a1047.t:
Un morceau de coltan
Aterian, société cotée à Londres, a annoncé le lancement d’opérations commerciales élargies au Rwanda, marquées par le transfert de la première livraison de concentré de tantale/niobium issu de sources responsables, également appelé coltan, à son partenaire commercial mondial.
L’entreprise a déclaré que son partenariat avec une importante société internationale de négoce de métaux et minéraux lui a fourni une plateforme commerciale et marketing mondiale bien établie. Cet accord a permis à Aterian d’accéder à un réseau d’acheteurs en aval et d’accélérer le développement de ses activités.
Aterian a expliqué le 15 septembre qu’avant le début des ventes commerciales, son partenaire avait procédé à des vérifications préalables et à des essais approfondis afin de tester la qualité et la conformité des produits.
Ces contrôles ont été effectués auprès d’un groupe de fournisseurs miniers artisanaux et à petite échelle au Rwanda, qui respectent les normes de l’Organisation de coopération et de développement économiques (OCDE).
Suite à la réussite de ce processus, Eastinco, filiale rwandaise à 100 % d’Aterian, a activé sa chaîne d’approvisionnement en tantale et niobium issus de sources responsables et a débuté ses activités commerciales.
Pour soutenir son expansion, Aterian a obtenu un prêt mezzanine de 250 000 dollars. L’entreprise a confirmé que les fonds avaient déjà été intégralement utilisés et investis dans des opérations de négoce, notamment pour l’acquisition de concentrés minéraux provenant du Rwanda.
« La réussite des essais et des contrôles de conformité des fournisseurs, combinée à l’injection de nouveaux capitaux de négoce, nous permet désormais d’avancer à un rythme soutenu. Nous prévoyons une augmentation significative des volumes de négoce au cours des prochaines semaines, grâce à l’activation de multiples relations d’approvisionnement et au renforcement des opérations d’approvisionnement avec nos partenaires financiers.
« Il s’agit d’un moment charnière pour notre activité de négoce, qui pose les bases commerciales de notre croissance dans la région. » « Grâce à nos opérations, à nos systèmes de gestion des risques et à nos partenariats désormais en place, nous sommes confiants dans notre capacité à démontrer une conformité totale en matière de traçabilité tout en bâtissant une chaîne d’approvisionnement robuste et intègre, capable de soutenir une croissance substantielle des volumes et de soutenir la génération de revenus à long terme pour le groupe », a déclaré Simon Rollason, PDG d’Aterian.
Aterian a déclaré que tous ses approvisionnements en minéraux provenaient de l’Initiative internationale pour la chaîne d’approvisionnement en étain et étaient pleinement conformes aux directives de l’OCDE en matière de diligence raisonnable. Cela impliquait des audits rigoureux sur site, la vérification de l’origine des mines et des contrôles d’absence de conflit afin de garantir la légitimité et l’intégrité de la chaîne d’approvisionnement.
L’entreprise a également souligné que chaque fournisseur était soumis à un processus d’intégration et d’audit détaillé couvrant les normes opérationnelles, juridiques et éthiques. Ces procédures comprenaient des évaluations sur site, la confirmation de l’origine des mines et la vérification du statut d’absence de conflit. Aterian a déclaré que ces contrôles se poursuivraient et étaient essentiels au maintien d’un approvisionnement régulier en matériaux.
Selon l’entreprise, le partenariat avec sa maison de négoce a validé son modèle économique et a ouvert une voie commerciale claire pour la mise en place d’une plateforme d’exploration et de négoce verticalement intégrée pour les minéraux critiques. Dans toute l’Afrique de l’Est.
L’engagement en faveur de la traçabilité et de l’approvisionnement responsable vise également à rassurer les acheteurs en aval, de plus en plus attentifs aux normes environnementales, sociales et de gouvernance.
Aterian a confirmé que les ventes à l’exportation, à l’échelle des conteneurs, étaient désormais prêtes à démarrer. (Fin)
a1047.en:
Aterian launches expanded commercial operations in Rwanda with its first coltan delivery

A piece of coltan

Aterian, a London-listed company, has announced the launch of expanded commercial operations in Rwanda, marked by the transfer of the first delivery of responsibly sourced tantalum/niobium concentrate, also known as coltan, to its global trading partner.

The company said that its partnership with a major international metals and minerals trading company provided it with a well-established global trading and marketing platform. This agreement allowed Aterian to access a network of downstream buyers and to accelerate the development of its activities.

Aterian explained on 15 September that, before commercial sales began, its partner had carried out prior verifications and extensive testing in order to test the quality and compliance of the products.

These checks were carried out with a group of artisanal and small-scale mining suppliers in Rwanda that comply with the standards of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Following the success of this process, Eastinco, Aterian's 100% Rwandan subsidiary, activated its supply chain of responsibly sourced tantalum and niobium and began its commercial activities.

To support its expansion, Aterian obtained a mezzanine loan of $250,000. The company confirmed that the funds had already been fully used and invested in trading operations, notably for the acquisition of mineral concentrates from Rwanda.

"The successful completion of testing and supplier compliance checks, combined with the injection of new trading capital, now allows us to move forward at a sustained pace. We anticipate a significant increase in trading volumes over the coming weeks, thanks to the activation of multiple supply relationships and the strengthening of sourcing operations with our financial partners.

"This is a pivotal moment for our trading business, which lays the commercial foundations for our growth in the region." "With our operations, our risk management systems and our partnerships now in place, we are confident in our ability to demonstrate full traceability compliance while building a robust supply chain with integrity, capable of supporting substantial volume growth and sustaining long-term revenue generation for the group," said Simon Rollason, CEO of Aterian.

Aterian said that all of its mineral supplies came from the International Tin Supply Chain Initiative and were fully compliant with the OECD's due diligence guidelines. This involved rigorous on-site audits, verification of the mine of origin, and conflict-free checks to guarantee the legitimacy and integrity of the supply chain.

The company also stressed that each supplier was subject to a detailed onboarding and audit process covering operational, legal and ethical standards. These procedures included on-site assessments, confirmation of the mine of origin and verification of conflict-free status. Aterian said these checks would continue and were essential to maintaining a regular supply of materials.

According to the company, the partnership with its trading house validated its business model and opened a clear commercial path for the establishment of a vertically integrated exploration and trading platform for critical minerals. Across East Africa.

The commitment to traceability and responsible sourcing is also intended to reassure downstream buyers, who are increasingly attentive to environmental, social and governance standards.

Aterian confirmed that export sales, at container scale, were now ready to begin. (End)

a1211.t:
La Côte d’Ivoire poursuit ses efforts dans le renforcement de la sécurité et de la gestion de ses frontières. Le lundi 22 septembre 2025, au Ministère de l’Intérieur et de la Sécurité, s’est tenue la cérémonie officielle de remise des clés du poste de police frontière de Kalamon, situé dans le département de Dorobo, région du Bounkani.
L’infrastructure, construite et équipée grâce à l’appui de l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM) et des États-Unis, a été symboliquement remise aux autorités ivoiriennes en présence du ministre de l’Intérieur et de la Sécurité, de l’ambassadrice des États-Unis en Côte d’Ivoire et du chef de mission de l’OIM.
Ce poste moderne s’inscrit dans le cadre du projet régional « Renforcer les frontières nord de la Côte d’Ivoire, du Ghana et du Togo », financé par le Département d’État américain. Il a été conçu pour améliorer le contrôle des mouvements transfrontaliers, lutter contre la criminalité transnationale et renforcer la coopération régionale en matière de sécurité et de gestion migratoire.
Le poste de Kalamon est doté d’équipements modernes : énergie solaire, forage hydraulique, infrastructures d’accueil pour les forces de sécurité, dispositifs de contrôle des passeports et de délivrance de visas. Il constitue, selon le chef de mission de l’OIM en Côte d’Ivoire, David Breux, « 𝑢𝑛 𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑙 𝑎𝑢 𝑠𝑒𝑟𝑣𝑖𝑐𝑒 𝑑𝑒 𝑙𝑎 𝑝𝑎𝑖𝑥, 𝑑𝑒 𝑙𝑎 𝑚𝑜𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑒́ 𝑒𝑡 𝑑𝑒 𝑙𝑎 𝑐𝑜𝑜𝑝𝑒́𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑠𝑓𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑒̀𝑟𝑒 ».
Au-delà de la sécurité, le projet a eu des retombées directes pour les communautés : plus de 2 800 pièces d’identité délivrées via des centres d’identification mobiles, la réhabilitation de la maternité de Doubasso, des campagnes de sensibilisation sur la cohésion sociale et l’alerte précoce, ainsi que l’amélioration d’infrastructures locales.
Pour l’ambassadrice des États-Unis en Côte d’Ivoire, Jessica Davis Ba, cette inauguration illustre « 𝑢𝑛𝑒 𝑐𝑜𝑜𝑝𝑒́𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑠𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑑𝑒 𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑒 𝑙𝑒 𝑝𝑒𝑢𝑝𝑙𝑒 𝑎𝑚𝑒́𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑖𝑛 𝑒𝑡 𝑙𝑒 𝑝𝑒𝑢𝑝𝑙𝑒 𝑖𝑣𝑜𝑖𝑟𝑖𝑒𝑛 ». Elle a souligné que la sécurité constitue la base du commerce, de l’investissement et de la prospérité partagée.
De son côté, Vagondo Diomandé, ministre de l’Intérieur et de la Sécurité a salué l’appui constant des partenaires internationaux, rappelant que ce poste frontalier est à la fois un symbole de souveraineté nationale et un levier de développement local et régional.
Les acteurs impliqués ambitionnent d’étendre cette dynamique à d’autres zones stratégiques du pays, afin de renforcer la présence de l’État aux frontières, améliorer la gestion des flux migratoires et consolider l’intégration régionale.
Avec ce nouveau poste frontalier, la Côte d’Ivoire réaffirme sa volonté de bâtir des frontières « 𝑜𝑢𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑡𝑒𝑠 𝑎̀ 𝑙𝑎 𝑝𝑎𝑖𝑥, 𝑎̀ 𝑙𝑎 𝑠𝑒́𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑖𝑡𝑒́ 𝑒𝑡 𝑎𝑢 𝑑𝑒́𝑣𝑒𝑙𝑜𝑝𝑝𝑒𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒́ », dans un contexte régional marqué par des défis sécuritaires persistants.
a1211.en:
Côte d'Ivoire is continuing its efforts to strengthen the security and management of its borders. On Monday 22 September 2025, at the Ministry of the Interior and Security, the official ceremony handing over the keys to the Kalamon border police post, located in the department of Dorobo, Bounkani region, was held.

The facility, built and equipped with the support of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United States, was symbolically handed over to the Ivorian authorities in the presence of the Minister of the Interior and Security, the United States Ambassador to Côte d'Ivoire and the IOM chief of mission.

This modern post is part of the regional project "Strengthening the northern borders of Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana and Togo," funded by the US State Department. It was designed to improve control of cross-border movements, combat transnational crime and strengthen regional cooperation on security and migration management.

The Kalamon post is equipped with modern facilities: solar power, a water borehole, reception infrastructure for the security forces, and passport control and visa issuance systems. According to the IOM chief of mission in Côte d'Ivoire, David Breux, it constitutes "a tool in the service of peace, mobility and cross-border cooperation."

Beyond security, the project has had direct benefits for local communities: more than 2,800 identity documents issued through mobile identification centres, the rehabilitation of the Doubasso maternity unit, awareness campaigns on social cohesion and early warning, as well as improvements to local infrastructure.

For the United States Ambassador to Côte d'Ivoire, Jessica Davis Ba, this inauguration illustrates "solid cooperation between the American people and the Ivorian people." She stressed that security is the foundation of trade, investment and shared prosperity.

For his part, Vagondo Diomandé, Minister of the Interior and Security, welcomed the constant support of international partners, recalling that this border post is both a symbol of national sovereignty and a lever for local and regional development.

The actors involved aim to extend this momentum to other strategic areas of the country, in order to strengthen the State's presence at the borders, improve the management of migration flows and consolidate regional integration.

With this new border post, Côte d'Ivoire reaffirms its determination to build borders "open to peace, security and shared development," in a regional context marked by persistent security challenges.

By Alick Ponje:
World Health Organisation (WHO) Director for Health Financing and Economics, Kalipso Chalkidou, has warned that the world is facing a health financing emergency.
Speaking at a regular press briefing for humanitarian agencies in Geneva, Switzerland, Chalkidou cautioned that as wealthier nations implement deep spending cuts, both international aid and national health systems are experiencing serious disruption.
She cited recent decisions by the United States (US), several European governments and European Union bodies to freeze or reduce health aid.
WHO forecasts suggest that global health investment is likely to fall by up to 40 percent this year, dropping by $10 billion from just over $25 billion in 2023.
- Advertisement -
“The estimated $15 billion spent on health aid would bring the figure down to the lowest level in a decade,” the health agency said.
It added that the funding shortfall is creating a health financing emergency in many developing countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, which depend on external aid to fund their health systems.
“In numerous countries, US-financed healthcare programmes were the primary source of external aid, accounting for as much as 30 percent of current health spending in countries like Malawi and around 25 percent in Mozambique and Zimbabwe,” WHO said.
The agency further raised concerns about rising debt burdens, saying many sub- Saharan African nations are grappling with soaring debt, with some spending twice as much on debt servicing as on health, making the reallocation of resources difficult.
- Advertisement -
- Advertisement -
It quoted Chalkidou referencing a WHO survey indicating that countries are now reporting health service disruptions “not seen since the peak of Covid-19”.
To address the crisis, WHO has urged countries to reduce aid dependency, increase revenue through improved taxation including health taxes on products like tobacco and alcohol, and collaborate with multilateral banks to secure low-interest loans for cost-effective health investments.
Following the abrupt withdrawal of support from the US Agency for International Development (USAid), Malawi is facing disruptions across its public health, economic and development sectors.
The exit has triggered a challenge particularly in healthcare, where preliminary reports suggest the impact has been both immediate and severe.
USAid’s funding was crucial in sustaining HIV treatment programmes, maternal health services and staffing at numerous clinics across the country.
The government, however, insists it is doing everything possible to bridge the gap left by the aid cuts, although thousands of people employed through USAid-funded initiatives have already lost their jobs.
Authorities have since called for a shift towards economic self-reliance, with an emphasis on entrepreneurship and partnerships with alternative international donors.

a1423.t:
L’organisation Muslim Charity rejoint le Fonds philanthropique islamique de l’Organisation internationale pour les migrations (Oim). Ils ont signé un nouveau protocole d’accord, concrétisé par le versement d’1 million de dollars pour soutenir les efforts mondiaux visant à mettre fin à la traite des êtres humains et à l’esclavage moderne. Cette collaboration marque le premier partenariat formel dans le cadre du Fonds de philanthropie islamique de l’Oim depuis son lancement au début de l’année.
Ce partenariat reflète un engagement commun à défendre la dignité humaine et la justice », a déclaré Mohammed Abdiker, chef de cabinet de l’Oim. « En fléchant les dons d’origine religieuse vers les initiatives mondiales visant à mettre fin à l’exploitation, nous répondons à des besoins urgents, et nous nous engageons sur la voie d’un changement durable. La solidarité peut se traduire par des actions concrètes pour ceux qui vivent dans l’ombre des conflits, de la pauvreté et des déplacements et le Fonds philanthropique islamique en est un parfait exemple. » On estime à 50 millions le nombre de personnes vivant dans des conditions d’esclavage moderne à travers le monde, chiffre qui comprend les survivants de la traite des êtres humains. Les enfants représentent près d’un tiers des victimes de la traite, tandis que la majorité des personnes prisonnières de ce système sont victimes de travail forcé et d’exploitation sexuelle. Alors que les déplacements de population dans le monde continuent d’augmenter en raison des conflits, des crises climatiques et de l’instabilité économique, le risque d’exploitation des personnes vulnérables devient de plus en plus grave.
« Il y a plus de 1 400 ans, le prophète Mahomet (que la paix soit sur lui) s’est battu pour l’abolition de l’esclavage et la préservation de la dignité humaine », a déclaré Irfan Rajput, directeur des programmes et de la politique pour Muslim Charity. « Inspirée par ces valeurs intemporelles, l’association Muslim Charity s’est engagée à combattre les causes profondes et les conséquences de l’esclavage moderne et de la traite des êtres humains. Grâce à ce partenariat avec l’OIM, nous faisons appel à la compassion et à la générosité de la communauté musulmane pour aider à libérer les personnes victimes d’exploitation et leur rendre leurs droits, leur dignité et leurs possibilités d’avenir. » Grâce à ce nouveau partenariat, Muslim Charity se joint à l’OIM et au Forum mondial des donateurs (Gdf) dans leurs efforts de prévention de la traite, de protection des survivants et de promotion des solutions durables pour les personnes et les communautés touchées. Cette contribution renforce également l’initiative conjointe avec le Forum mondial des donateurs et aidera l’Oim dans son travail en Afghanistan, où le soutien est principalement axé sur le renforcement de la résilience des communautés et sur l’amélioration de l’accès aux services essentiels pour les populations déplacées et rapatriées. Par cet accord, l’expertise mondiale de l’Oim en matière d’aide humanitaire et de protection se voit renforcée par le travail de Muslim Charity, qui cible l’aide d’urgence et les solutions de développement durable. La collaboration est ancrée dans les principes islamiques, notamment la Zakat, la Sadaqah et le concept de Riqab, qui prône l’obligation de soutenir les personnes victimes d’exploitation et d’abus. Créé en 2025, le Fonds philanthropique islamique de l’OIM vise à utiliser les dons d’origine religieuse pour soutenir les personnes touchées par les déplacements, la traite et d’autres formes de vulnérabilité. Le Fonds fonctionne selon une politique de distribution de la Zakat à 100 % afin de garantir que chaque contribution bénéficie directement aux personnes dans le besoin, conformément aux valeurs islamiques de confiance et de responsabilité. La collaboration avec Muslim Charity marque une étape importante dans l’utilisation de financements sociaux islamiques pour protéger les populations vulnérables et défendre leurs droits. À mesure que le Fonds de philanthropie islamique se développera, l’OIM continuera à établir des partenariats stratégiques avec des institutions caritatives, des organisations religieuses et des donateurs individuels afin d’élargir son impact.
Fifonsi Cyrience KOUGNANDE
a1423.en:
The organization Muslim Charity is joining the Islamic Philanthropy Fund of the International Organization for Migration (IOM). They have signed a new memorandum of understanding, made concrete by the payment of $1 million to support global efforts to end human trafficking and modern slavery. This collaboration marks the first formal partnership under IOM's Islamic Philanthropy Fund since its launch at the beginning of the year.

"This partnership reflects a shared commitment to defending human dignity and justice," said Mohammed Abdiker, IOM Chief of Staff. "By directing faith-based donations toward global initiatives aimed at ending exploitation, we are responding to urgent needs, and we are setting out on the path to lasting change. Solidarity can translate into concrete action for those living in the shadow of conflict, poverty and displacement, and the Islamic Philanthropy Fund is a perfect example of this." An estimated 50 million people are living in conditions of modern slavery around the world, a figure that includes survivors of human trafficking. Children account for nearly one third of trafficking victims, while the majority of people trapped in this system are victims of forced labour and sexual exploitation. As population displacement around the world continues to increase because of conflict, climate crises and economic instability, the risk of exploitation of vulnerable people is becoming ever more serious.

"More than 1,400 years ago, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) fought for the abolition of slavery and the preservation of human dignity," said Irfan Rajput, Director of Programmes and Policy for Muslim Charity. "Inspired by these timeless values, Muslim Charity has committed itself to combating the root causes and the consequences of modern slavery and human trafficking. Through this partnership with IOM, we are calling on the compassion and generosity of the Muslim community to help free people who are victims of exploitation and to restore to them their rights, their dignity and their opportunities for the future." Through this new partnership, Muslim Charity joins IOM and the Global Donors Forum (GDF) in their efforts to prevent trafficking, protect survivors and promote sustainable solutions for the people and communities affected. This contribution also strengthens the joint initiative with the Global Donors Forum and will help IOM in its work in Afghanistan, where support is mainly focused on strengthening the resilience of communities and on improving access to essential services for displaced and returnee populations. Through this agreement, IOM's global expertise in humanitarian assistance and protection is reinforced by the work of Muslim Charity, which targets emergency aid and sustainable development solutions. The collaboration is rooted in Islamic principles, in particular Zakat, Sadaqah and the concept of Riqab, which upholds the obligation to support people who are victims of exploitation and abuse. Created in 2025, IOM's Islamic Philanthropy Fund aims to use faith-based donations to support people affected by displacement, trafficking and other forms of vulnerability. The Fund operates under a 100% Zakat distribution policy in order to guarantee that every contribution directly benefits people in need, in accordance with the Islamic values of trust and accountability. The collaboration with Muslim Charity marks an important step in the use of Islamic social financing to protect vulnerable populations and defend their rights. As the Islamic Philanthropy Fund develops, IOM will continue to establish strategic partnerships with charitable institutions, faith-based organizations and individual donors in order to broaden its impact.
